Difficulty: Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, then hates and discards her; Absalom murders Amnon in revenge; David, though angry, does nothing. Readers ask why Scripture includes sexual violence at the heart of David's house, and why David's passivity goes unpunished in the chapter.
Explanations: The agreed reading is descriptive: the chapter is part of Nathan's announced consequence — 'the sword shall never depart from thine house' (2 Samuel 12:10) — working itself out in David's own family. Tamar is given voice and dignity in the text (her protest, her torn robe, her ashes), Amnon's lust is named as hatred after the act, and Absalom's revenge, though understandable as a brother's anger, starts a rebellion that will tear the kingdom. David's failure to act is itself presented as a failure, with catastrophic consequences, not as something God overlooks.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The passage sides with Tamar and exposes the men around her. Its horror is the fruit of David's own sin returning to his house, exactly as Nathan said it would.
